item.title: Who We Are
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
St. Columba Parish is a Roman Catholic community of the Archdiocese of Toronto, rooted at the corner of Columba Avenue and Pape in East York. About 1,200 households call this their parish home. Some have been here since the church was dedicated in 1961; others arrived last month. Whether you are a lifelong Catholic, someone returning after years away, or simply curious, this page will tell you who we are and how to find your place among us.

A welcome from our pastor

Dear friends,

Thank you for visiting St. Columba, whether in person or through this website. A parish is not a building or a schedule of services. It is a family of people who gather around the altar every week, carry one another through sickness and loss, celebrate births and weddings together, and try, in an ordinary Toronto neighbourhood, to live as Jesus asked us to.

You will hear Mass here in English, Spanish, Tagalog and Italian, and you will meet families from Portugal, Sri Lanka, Nigeria, Ireland and dozens of other places. What unites us is far greater than what distinguishes us. If you are new, please introduce yourself after Mass. I would very much like to meet you.

In Christ,
Rev. Daniel Moreau
Pastor

The parish at a glance

1954 year founded
1,200 registered families
6 language communities
30+ ministries and groups

We celebrate seven Masses every weekend and one every weekday, hear confessions twice a week, and keep the church open for Adoration on Thursday mornings. The parish hall seats 220 people and hosts everything from First Communion breakfasts to the Knights' pasta dinner. See the full Mass and confession schedule or browse the ministry directory.

Our mission

St. Columba Parish exists to worship God, to form missionary disciples, and to serve our neighbours in East York with the love of Christ. We do this by celebrating the sacraments well, teaching the faith at every age, welcoming every person who walks through our doors, and sharing what we have with those who have less.

In practice, that mission takes the shape of a Sunday choir that has sung together for thirty years, a St. Vincent de Paul conference that visits about forty households a month, a youth group that fills the hall on Friday nights, and a catechetical program that prepares roughly ninety children a year for First Communion and Confirmation. Our 2025–2028 pastoral plan sets out where we hope to be in three years.

Our patron

Columba (521–597) was an Irish monk who founded the monastery of Iona and brought the Gospel to Scotland. The Irish families who built this parish chose him as a patron for a community of immigrants: a saint who left home to carry the faith somewhere new.

— St. Columba, pray for us. Feast day June 9

Our neighbourhood

East York was its own borough until amalgamation in 1998, and it still feels like a small town inside the city: brick semis, corner bakeries, the Danforth a short walk south. The parish sits a few blocks from Pape Station, with the parking lot behind the hall and a TTC stop at the door.

Our boundaries run roughly from the Don Valley east to Coxwell Avenue and from the Danforth north to O'Connor Drive, but you are welcome here wherever you live. Many parishioners drive in from Scarborough, Leaside and downtown because their family has always come, or because they found a community here.

Two Toronto Catholic District School Board schools sit within the parish, and we share a chaplaincy relationship with both. See our parish school page.

Find us

St. Columba Parish, 1240 Columba Avenue, Toronto, ON M4K 2R6
Office Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM–4:00 PM (closed 12–1) · 416-555-0142 · office@stcolumbatoronto.ca
Accessible entrance on the east side, elevator to the hall, hearing loop in the church. Details on our accessibility page.

Where to go next

If this is your first visit, start with our guide for newcomers. If you already know your way around, check the Mass schedule or find a group to join. Questions of any kind are welcome at the parish office, or ask any usher on Sunday.

item.title: Accessibility
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Everyone belongs at Mass. St. Columba Parish is committed to providing its services in a way that respects the dignity and independence of people with disabilities, and to meeting the requirements of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA) and the standards made under it. Our building dates from 1954, and we have been steadily adapting it since; the hearing loop, elevator and accessible washroom were added in 2019 through a parish campaign and a grant from the Archdiocese. Where a barrier remains, we will do our best to work around it with you.

Getting into the church and hall

  • Accessible entrance on the east side of the church (facing the parking lot), with a level path from the sidewalk, an automatic door opener and no steps. The main front doors have six steps and a handrail.
  • Elevator just inside the east entrance serving the church level, the lower-level parish hall and the washrooms.
  • Accessible washroom on the lower level beside the elevator, with an adult change bench and an emergency call button; a second accessible washroom is off the church vestibule.
  • Accessible parking: four designated spaces beside the east entrance. On Sundays the first row of the lot is reserved for people with mobility needs; ushers will direct you.
  • Drop-off: the east-side driveway loop allows drivers to stop at the door.

Inside the church

  • Pew cut-outs for wheelchairs and scooters at the front and back of the centre aisle and on both side aisles, so you can sit with your family rather than apart from them.
  • Hearing loop covering the whole nave. Switch your hearing aid or cochlear implant to the "T" setting. Loop receivers with headphones are available from the ushers for anyone without a T-coil.
  • Large-print missals and hymn sheets in the rack at each entrance, and large-print copies of the bulletin at the office.
  • Lighting on the sanctuary and ambo was upgraded in 2023 to reduce glare; the readings are also projected on the screens at the 11:00 AM Mass.
  • Seating with arms in the last three rows on each side, and a small number of chairs with higher seats at the back for anyone who finds pews difficult.
  • Service animals are welcome everywhere in the church and hall.

Taking part in Mass

Holy Communion is brought to anyone who cannot come forward. Simply stay in your pew and raise a hand, or let an usher know before Mass; a minister will come to you. Gluten-free (low-gluten) hosts are available; tell the priest or an usher before Mass and receive from the priest's line. The Sunday 11:00 AM Mass is livestreamed and archived for those who cannot attend in person. Confession is available in the reconciliation room, which is on the level of the church and large enough for a wheelchair, as well as in the traditional confessional.

If you or a family member has a disability that affects sacramental preparation, for example a child on the autism spectrum preparing for First Communion, please speak with Sr. Agnes (ext. 25). We have adapted materials and experience, and no one is excluded from the sacraments because of a disability.

Parish hall

The hall is reached by the elevator or the interior stairs, has a level floor, an accessible washroom, wide doors and an accessible route to the stage by ramp. Tables are set at wheelchair height on request. See Hall Rentals if you are planning an event.

Website accessibility

This website is designed to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA, the standard Ontario requires of public-facing websites. In practice that means:

  • All text can be resized to 200 per cent without losing content, and the site works at phone width.
  • Every image has a text description, and decorative images are hidden from screen readers.
  • All pages can be navigated by keyboard alone, with a visible focus indicator and a "skip to content" link.
  • Colour contrast meets the AA minimum, and colour is never the only way information is conveyed.
  • Videos on the livestream page carry captions where the source provides them.
  • Bulletins are posted as PDFs; if you need a bulletin in another format, the office will email you the text.

We test the site with a screen reader and keyboard each time it is redesigned, but we know issues can slip through. If you find a page that does not work for you, please tell us using the feedback process below and we will fix it as quickly as we can.

Feedback and requests

  1. Tell us

    Call 416-555-0142 ext. 21, email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "Accessibility" in the subject line, use the contact form, or speak to any usher or staff member. We accept feedback in any format, including in person or by mail.

  2. We acknowledge it

    You will hear back within five business days, in the format you prefer.

  3. We act

    Small fixes, such as a website issue or a missing large-print missal, are handled right away. Larger requests go to the pastor and the Finance Council; we will tell you what we can do and when.

Documents such as this policy, our privacy policy and registration forms are available on request in large print or by email. Our accessibility contact is Teresa Alvarez, Office Manager. For information about the AODA and your rights under it, see ontario.ca/accessibility.

Frequently asked

Can someone meet me at the door?

Yes. Call the office ahead of time or ask a greeter, and an usher will meet you at the east entrance and help you to a seat.

Is there a quiet space if my child becomes overwhelmed?

The vestibule cry room at the back of the church has a window and speaker so you can still follow Mass. It is open at every Mass.

Do you offer Mass in sign language?

Not at St. Columba at present. The Archdiocese supports a Deaf ministry with interpreted Masses at a downtown parish; the office can give you the details.

item.title: Archdiocese of Toronto
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
A parish is never an island. St. Columba belongs to the Archdiocese of Toronto, the family of Catholic parishes, schools, hospitals, cemeteries and charities that stretches from Lake Ontario north to Georgian Bay and from Oshawa west to Mississauga. The Archdiocese is led by the Archbishop of Toronto, assisted by auxiliary bishops, and it serves close to two million Catholics who worship in more than three dozen languages every Sunday. Our parish shares in that wider mission, and the offices of the Archdiocese in turn support the work we do here in East York.

What the Archdiocese is

In the Catholic Church, a diocese is a territory entrusted to a bishop, who is the chief teacher, shepherd and priest of the local Church. Because Toronto is a metropolitan see, its bishop holds the title of Archbishop. The Archbishop of Toronto appoints and assigns priests, oversees the seminary, approves parish boundaries and building projects, and is responsible for the teaching of the faith across the whole region. The chancery (the Catholic Pastoral Centre downtown) houses the offices that coordinate everything from marriage tribunals and Catholic education to refugee sponsorship and youth ministry.

The cathedral of the Archdiocese is St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica on Bond Street. Every parish is invited to the Chrism Mass held there in Holy Week, when the Archbishop blesses the holy oils that we use at baptisms, confirmations, ordinations and anointings throughout the year.

How our parish relates to the Archdiocese

Fr. Moreau and Fr. Nguyen are priests of the Archdiocese, assigned to St. Columba by the Archbishop. Deacon Ferreira was ordained by the Archbishop for service in this region. Our parish follows archdiocesan policy on finances, volunteer screening, sacramental records and safe environment, and we file an annual financial report with the chancery. In practical terms, this means a few things for you as a parishioner:

  • Your donations are receipted under our own charitable registration, but online giving runs through the secure archdiocesan portal.
  • Sacramental records (baptisms, confirmations, marriages) are kept here and copied to the archdiocesan archive, so a certificate can be found even decades later.
  • Marriage annulment cases, permissions for mixed marriages and dispensations are handled by the archdiocesan Marriage Tribunal and Chancery, with our clergy helping you prepare the paperwork.
  • Our parish pays an annual assessment to the Archdiocese that funds the seminary, retired priests, chaplaincies and central services.

Good to know

St. Columba is part of the Central Region of the Archdiocese, and belongs to a deanery of neighbouring East York and Riverdale parishes whose pastors meet monthly. If you move within the Archdiocese, your sacramental records stay searchable, and you can simply register at your new parish.

Services

Archdiocesan offices and services

Many of the ministries that touch parish life are run centrally. These are the ones parishioners ask about most often.

Pastoral care

Chaplaincies

Catholic chaplains serve Toronto's hospitals, universities, prisons and long-term-care homes. Learn how to request a chaplain for a loved one.

Chaplaincies

ORAT

Refugee Sponsorship

The Office for Refugees helps parishes like ours welcome families fleeing persecution. Our sponsorship committee is always looking for help.

Refugee sponsorship

Office of Vocations

Vocations

Discerning priesthood, the permanent diaconate or consecrated life? The Office of Vocations and our parish can walk with you.

Vocations

External

Catholic Cemeteries & Funeral Services

The Archdiocese operates Catholic cemeteries across the region, including Mount Hope and Holy Cross, and offers pre-planning consultations.

catholic-cemeteries.ca

External

ShareLife

The annual archdiocesan appeal funds more than 40 agencies serving families, seniors, newcomers and people with disabilities. Our parish goal is set each spring.

sharelife.org

External

Formation for Discipleship

Courses, retreats and resources for adults who want to grow in faith and lead in their parish, offered by the Archdiocese.

archtoronto.org

Policy

Safe Environment

The Strengthening the Caring Community policy sets out how every parish protects children and vulnerable adults, and how concerns are reported.

Safe environment

Frequently asked

Can I attend Mass at any parish in the Archdiocese?

Yes. You may worship anywhere, and your Sunday obligation is fulfilled at any Catholic Mass. Registering with one parish simply lets us serve you well with envelopes, sacramental preparation and records.

Where do I get a copy of a baptism certificate from another Toronto parish?

Contact the parish where the baptism took place. If that church has closed or merged, the Archdiocesan Archives holds its registers; our office can tell you who to call.

How does the Archbishop visit parishes?

The Archbishop or an auxiliary bishop comes to St. Columba for Confirmation each spring and for anniversaries and special occasions. Pastoral visits are announced in the bulletin well ahead of time.

Questions about anything on this page? Contact Ann Marie O'Connor at the parish office, 416-555-0142 ext. 20, or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca, and we will point you to the right archdiocesan office.

Visit archtoronto.org

item.title: Becoming Catholic (OCIA)
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Every year a dozen or so adults are baptized, received into the Church or confirmed at St. Columba's Easter Vigil. Some married a Catholic and grew curious. Some were baptized as babies and never went further. Some walked in off Pape Avenue one Sunday and kept coming back. Whatever brought you here, the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, or OCIA (until 2021 it was called RCIA), is the path the Church offers. It is unhurried, it is free, and it begins with nothing more than a conversation.

Who OCIA is for

Never baptized

Adults seeking baptism

If you have never been baptized in any Christian church, OCIA prepares you to receive Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion together at the Easter Vigil. You are called a catechumen once you formally enter the process.

Baptized in another church

Christians becoming Catholic

If you were baptized Anglican, United, Baptist, Orthodox or in another Christian tradition, the Church recognizes your baptism. You prepare to make a profession of faith and receive Confirmation and Communion. You are called a candidate.

Baptized Catholic

Catholics completing their sacraments

If you were baptized Catholic but never made your First Communion or were never confirmed, OCIA is for you too. Many in the group each year are in exactly this situation, often in their twenties, thirties or forties.

The stages

The process follows four stages with a liturgical rite marking the passage from each to the next. Most people move through it in one year, but nobody is held to a calendar; if you need longer, you take longer.

  1. Inquiry (September to November)

    Come and ask questions. The first weeks are open conversations about God, Jesus, prayer, the Church and whatever is on your mind. Nothing is signed. If you decide this is not for you, you leave with our thanks and no hard feelings.

  2. Catechumenate (December to February)

    At the Rite of Acceptance, celebrated at a Sunday Mass in late November, you are welcomed by the parish and begin structured teaching on the Creed, the sacraments, the moral life and prayer. You attend Sunday Mass and are dismissed after the homily to reflect on the readings with your catechist.

  3. Purification and enlightenment (Lent)

    On the first Sunday of Lent, the Archbishop of Toronto or his delegate celebrates the Rite of Election at the cathedral for all the catechumens of the Archdiocese, and your name is written in the Book of the Elect. Lent is a retreat: fewer lessons, more prayer, three "scrutinies" at Sunday Mass, and a day of reflection in March.

  4. Sacraments at the Easter Vigil, then mystagogy

    On Holy Saturday night you are baptized and confirmed and receive Communion for the first time, in a church full of candles and parishioners who have been praying for you. The weeks of Easter that follow, called mystagogy, are for unpacking what happened and finding your place in the parish.

When and where we meet

Tuesdays, 7:00–8:30 PM, in the rectory meeting room, from the second Tuesday of September until the Easter Vigil. Sessions are led by Sr. Agnes Ibeh with a team of four parish catechists and Fr. Nguyen, who joins most weeks. Coffee and tea are on; some people come straight from work. There are no sessions during Christmas week or March Break. Reading material is provided, and there is no charge of any kind.

You may join at any point during the inquiry stage. If you find us in February, come anyway; we will talk about the best way forward for you.

Sponsors

Every catechumen and candidate has a sponsor, a practising Catholic who walks beside you, sits with you at Mass, answers the questions you are embarrassed to ask in the group, and stands with you at the Vigil. If you already know a Catholic you would like to ask, wonderful; a spouse cannot serve as a sponsor for baptism, but a friend or in-law can. If you do not know anyone, the parish will match you with a trained sponsor from the OCIA team. Sponsors complete the Archdiocese's volunteer screening.

Children and teenagers

OCIC: initiation for children of school age

Children aged seven to sixteen who have not been baptized, or who were baptized but have missed First Communion or Confirmation, are prepared through a parallel process on Sunday mornings during the school year, in age-appropriate groups. Parents attend several sessions with them. Younger children are baptized through the ordinary infant baptism preparation. Contact Sr. Agnes to discuss which path fits your child.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to decide to become Catholic before I start?

No. The inquiry stage exists precisely so that you can look before you commit. Some people take two years; some decide the Catholic Church is not for them, and part as friends.

I was married outside the Church, or I am divorced. Is that a problem?

It is a common situation and usually workable, but it needs to be looked at early. Please mention it in your first conversation with Sr. Agnes or Fr. Nguyen so that any steps, such as having a marriage blessed or seeking an annulment, can start in good time.

Do I need to attend Mass during OCIA?

Yes, from the Rite of Acceptance onward. Sunday Mass is where the parish meets Christ, and it is the best classroom there is. Most people find the 11:00 AM Mass works well because the group is dismissed together after the homily.

What documents will I need?

If you were baptized in another church, a copy of your baptismal certificate or a letter from that church. If you are unbaptized, nothing. Catholics completing their sacraments need a recent baptismal certificate from the parish of baptism; we can help you request it.

What happens after Easter?

You are a full member of the parish, with every ministry open to you. Most of last year's group are now lectors, hospitality ministers, or on the OCIA team themselves.

Take the first step

Contact Sr. Agnes Ibeh, SSND, Pastoral Associate and Catechetical Coordinator, at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca or 416-555-0142 ext. 25. She will suggest a time to meet for half an hour, in person or by phone, to hear your story and answer your questions. That conversation commits you to nothing.

item.title: Beliefs & Teachings
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
This page is not a textbook. It is a map: the main things the Catholic Church believes, each in a paragraph or two, with a pointer to where the full teaching can be read. If you are exploring the faith, it will give you the shape of it. If you were raised Catholic and want to understand what you already practise, it may connect a few dots. Where we say "the Church teaches," the authoritative source is the Catechism of the Catholic Church, which is free to read online.

The Creed

Every Sunday the whole congregation stands and says the Nicene Creed, a summary of the faith agreed by the bishops of the world in the fourth century. Its main affirmations are these:

  • One God in three Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, who created everything that exists.
  • Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who took on human flesh through the Virgin Mary, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, died and was buried, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven.
  • The Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets and gives life to the Church.
  • The Church, which is one, holy, catholic (meaning universal) and apostolic (founded on the apostles and led by their successors, the bishops in union with the Pope).
  • One baptism for the forgiveness of sins.
  • The resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.

The shorter Apostles' Creed, used in the Rosary and at baptisms, is on our prayers page.

The seven sacraments

A sacrament is a visible sign, instituted by Christ, through which God gives grace. There are seven. Baptism makes us children of God and members of the Church. Confirmation strengthens us with the Holy Spirit. The Eucharist feeds us with the Body and Blood of Christ. Reconciliation (confession) forgives sins committed after baptism. Anointing of the Sick brings Christ's healing to the seriously ill. Marriage unites a man and a woman in a lifelong covenant. Holy Orders ordains deacons, priests and bishops to serve the Church.

Each sacrament, and how to receive it here, is explained on our sacraments pages.

The Mass and the Eucharist

The Mass is the centre of Catholic life. In it, the Church does what Jesus commanded at the Last Supper: takes bread and wine, gives thanks, and shares them in his memory. Catholics believe that at the words of consecration the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ, while keeping the appearance of bread and wine; the Church's word for this is transubstantiation. That is why we kneel, why we keep the consecrated Hosts in the tabernacle with a lamp burning beside it, and why we set aside Thursday mornings for Adoration. Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday and holy day, and to receive Communion at least once a year at Easter time, though most receive every week. Our full schedule is on Mass times.

Mary and the saints

Catholics do not worship Mary or the saints; worship belongs to God alone. We honour them and ask for their prayers, as you might ask a friend to pray for you. Mary holds a unique place as the Mother of Jesus. The Church teaches that she was conceived without sin (the Immaculate Conception), remained a virgin, and at the end of her life was taken body and soul into heaven (the Assumption). The saints are men and women whom the Church has recognized as being with God, and whose lives show us that holiness is possible in every century and every walk of life. Our parish honours St. Columba, and our language communities keep the feasts of Our Lady of Fátima, San Lorenzo Ruiz and Our Lady of Guadalupe. See devotions.

Catholic social teaching

Faith that does not change how we treat other people is not the faith of the Gospel. Over the past 130 years the popes have set out principles for a just society, which the Church calls its social teaching:

  • The dignity of the human person — every life is sacred, from conception to natural death, regardless of ability, status or usefulness.
  • The common good — society is judged by whether it lets everyone flourish, not only the fortunate.
  • Solidarity — we are one human family, responsible for one another across borders and generations.
  • Subsidiarity — decisions should be made at the most local level that can make them well.
  • A preferential option for the poor — the needs of the poor and vulnerable come first.
  • The dignity of work — work serves people, not the other way round; workers have a right to fair wages and to organize.
  • Care for creation — the earth is a gift to be stewarded, not a resource to be used up.

At St. Columba this teaching takes shape in the St. Vincent de Paul conference, our refugee sponsorship group, the annual ShareLife appeal, and the work of Development and Peace, the Canadian Church's international development agency. See outreach.

Recommended resources

Catechism of the Catholic Church

The complete, official summary of Catholic teaching, searchable by topic and paragraph number. Start with Part One if you want the beliefs, Part Two for the sacraments, Part Three for the moral life, Part Four for prayer.

Read online at vatican.va

FORMED

Video series, audio talks, films and children's programs on the faith. St. Columba has a parish subscription, so parishioners can sign up free using the parish name and postal code.

formed.org

Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops

Statements, pastoral letters and resources from the bishops of Canada, including materials on reconciliation with Indigenous peoples and Catholic responses to public questions.

cccb.ca

Daily readings

The Scripture readings for each day's Mass from Living with Christ, the Canadian missalette used in our pews.

readings.livingwithchrist.ca

United States Conference of Catholic Bishops

A large English-language library on the Bible, the sacraments and Catholic social teaching, with the full text of the Bible online.

usccb.org

Archdiocese of Toronto

Our own diocese: news, the Cardinal's letters, Formation for Discipleship courses for adults, and directories of parishes and services.

archtoronto.org

Parishioners also recommend the books and videos of Bishop Robert Barron's Word on Fire ministry, several of which are in the parish lending library in the hall foyer.

Questions about any of this are welcome. Email Sr. Agnes Ibeh at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca, or, if you are ready for something more structured, read about Becoming Catholic and faith formation for adults.

item.title: Chaplaincies
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
When someone is in hospital, in a care home, in prison or living away from home at university, the Church goes to them. The Archdiocese of Toronto assigns priests, deacons and trained lay chaplains to institutions across the city, and every parish, including ours, shares in that care through its own pastoral visitors. This page explains what each chaplaincy does and, most importantly, how to reach one when you need it.

Hospital chaplaincy

Every major Toronto hospital has a spiritual care department, and Catholic chaplains, some of them priests, most of them trained lay ministers, deacons or religious sisters, work within it. A Catholic chaplain can bring Holy Communion, pray with you, arrange for a priest to hear your confession or anoint you, and sit with your family in difficult moments. Toronto also has a network of on-call priests so that anointing is available at any hour.

How to request a Catholic chaplain

  1. Tell the hospital you are Catholic

    Privacy law means the hospital will not tell any church who has been admitted. When you or your family member is registered, ask that "Roman Catholic" be recorded and that you would like a visit from the Catholic chaplain.

  2. Ask the nurse or the switchboard for Spiritual Care

    Any nurse can page the spiritual care department. Tell them what you need: Communion, a conversation, or a priest for anointing. Outside office hours the on-call priest is reached the same way.

  3. Let the parish know too

    Call the office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. We will add the name to the sick list if you wish, and one of our priests or Lay Pastoral Visitors will visit if the hospital is nearby.

Anointing of the Sick is not only for the dying

The sacrament is for anyone seriously ill, facing surgery or weakened by age, and it can be received more than once. Do not wait for the last hours. If you are going into hospital for a planned procedure, ask for anointing at St. Columba before you go. See Anointing of the Sick for details.

Long-term-care and home visits

Residents of nursing homes and retirement residences in our neighbourhood are visited by our clergy and Lay Pastoral Visitors on a monthly rotation, with a Communion service or Mass in the residence's common room. If your parent or spouse has moved into a care home anywhere in the Archdiocese, the parish that covers that address will take over visits; our office can make the introduction so no one falls through the cracks.

Parishioners who are housebound can receive Communion at home every week. Ask the office to arrange a Lay Pastoral Visitor, or speak to Deacon Ferreira after Mass.

University and college chaplaincy

The Archdiocese supports Catholic chaplaincies at the universities and colleges in Toronto, best known through the Newman Centre near the downtown campus, and through campus ministry teams at the other universities and colleges across the region. Chaplaincies offer Sunday and weekday Mass on or near campus, confession, retreats, faith-sharing groups, meals and a place to belong far from home. If a young person from our parish is heading to school this fall, encourage them to find the Catholic chaplaincy in the first week; students who connect early are far more likely to keep their faith through their studies.

Students home for the summer and Christmas are always welcome at our 5:00 PM Sunday youth and young adult Mass and at Young Adults events. Marcus Lee (youth@stcolumbatoronto.ca) can also connect students with campus ministers he knows.

Prison chaplaincy

Catholic chaplains serve the detention centres and correctional institutions in and around Toronto, celebrating Mass, leading Bible study and offering one-to-one support to inmates and, often, to their families. If a family member is incarcerated, they can ask to see the Catholic chaplain through the institution's chaplaincy office. Our St. Vincent de Paul conference also quietly supports families affected by incarceration; contact them through the office.

Our Lay Pastoral Visitors

St. Columba's Lay Pastoral Visitors are parishioners commissioned by the pastor to bring Holy Communion and the prayers of the parish to the sick, the housebound and residents of local care homes. There are currently fourteen visitors, and they serve about sixty people a month. Each has completed archdiocesan training, volunteer screening with a police vulnerable-sector check, and an annual refresher on privacy and boundaries.

  • What they do: a weekly or bi-weekly visit of 20 to 40 minutes, a short rite of Communion, prayer, and news from the parish, including the bulletin.
  • What they do not do: give medical or financial advice, handle money, or hear confessions; they will happily arrange a priest for those needs.
  • Who coordinates: Margaret Ferreira-Silva, pastoralcare@stcolumbatoronto.ca, through the parish office.

Would you like to become a visitor? We look for people who are steady, discreet and comfortable with silence. Training runs each October and February. See Volunteer and Volunteer Screening for what is involved.

Frequently asked

My mother is in hospital tonight. Who do I call for a priest?

Ask the nurse to page Spiritual Care and request the Catholic on-call priest; every Toronto hospital has one. Then call our office; if it is after hours, the voicemail gives the emergency number for our clergy.

Can a Lay Pastoral Visitor come to a retirement residence outside the parish?

Our visitors cover the residences within our parish boundaries. For others, we will contact that parish's pastoral care team on your behalf.

Is there a cost?

No. Chaplaincy and pastoral visiting are free. Families sometimes wish to make a donation to the parish afterwards, and that is welcome but never expected.

Questions? Contact the parish office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

item.title: Hall Rentals
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
St. Columba's parish hall sits on the lower level of the church, reached by the east-side accessible entrance and elevator or by the interior stairs from the vestibule. Renovated in 2019, it has a sprung hardwood floor, a stage, a full commercial kitchen and seating for 220 at round tables or 300 in rows. Parish groups use it most weekday evenings, but weekends and daytimes are often available for families and community groups. Baptism and First Communion receptions, wedding receptions, funeral luncheons, milestone birthdays, cultural association gatherings and neighbourhood meetings all find a home here.

The space

  • Main hall: about 4,200 square feet, 12-foot ceilings, hardwood floor, seating for 220 at tables (24 round tables of 8 to 10) or 300 in theatre rows.
  • Stage: 24 by 14 feet with a ramp, stage lighting, a lectern and a sound system with two wireless microphones; a projector and 12-foot screen are available.
  • Kitchen: commercial six-burner range, two ovens, warming cabinet, two fridges, a chest freezer, dishwasher and ample counter space. Suitable for caterers or for cooking on site.
  • Bar area with a service counter and ice machine.
  • Accessible: level entry from the elevator, accessible washroom, wide doors, ramp to the stage; see Accessibility.
  • Meeting room: a separate 30-seat room beside the hall, available on its own for smaller gatherings.
  • Parking for 60 cars in the church lot, plus street parking.

Rates

Rates are set by the Finance Council and reviewed each January. A registered parishioner is anyone whose household is on our parish roll; see Register with the Parish. Funeral luncheons for parishioners are offered at no charge (a donation is welcome).

Registered not-for-profit community groups may request the parishioner rate. A $100 non-refundable deposit confirms your date; the balance and the damage deposit are due 14 days before the event. Payment by cheque, e-transfer or debit at the office.

What is included

Every booking includes tables and chairs (set up by our custodian to your floor plan, submitted a week ahead), the sound system and microphones, use of washrooms and the coat room, heating and air conditioning, and a walk-through with Luis Ortega, our custodian, before the event. Tablecloths, dishes and cutlery are not included; caterers usually supply these, or you may rent our stock of 220 white place settings for $1.50 per setting.

Rules for renters

  1. Alcohol

    Alcohol may be served only with a Special Occasion Permit from the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, obtained by the renter and posted at the event, and only by a Smart Serve certified bartender. A copy of the permit must be on file at the office seven days before the event. No alcohol may be sold without the permit's sale endorsement.

  2. Insurance

    Non-parishioner renters and any event serving alcohol must provide a certificate of liability insurance for $2 million naming St. Columba Parish and the Archdiocese of Toronto as additional insureds. Event insurance for a single day is available from most brokers for roughly $100 to $200, and the office can suggest providers.

  3. Hours and noise

    Music ends at 11:30 PM and the hall must be vacated by midnight. Our neighbours are close; please keep the east doors closed during amplified music.

  4. Cleanup

    Renters remove all decorations, food and garbage (bagged and placed in the bins in the loading area), wipe tables, and leave the kitchen as they found it. Our custodian handles floors and washrooms. The damage deposit is returned within two weeks if the hall is left in good order.

  5. Respect for the space

    The hall is part of a church. No open flames other than sternos, no confetti or glitter, no tape or tacks on painted walls (use the hanging rails), no smoking or cannabis anywhere on the property, and no events that conflict with Catholic teaching or the parish's mission. The pastor has the final say on any booking.

Availability

The hall is not available on Sunday mornings, during Holy Week, or on Christmas Eve and Day. Saturday evenings book up three to six months ahead, and June and December are our busiest months. Parish groups have first call on weekday evenings.

How to book

  1. Send an inquiry using the form below, or call Ann Marie O'Connor at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. Tell us the date, the kind of event and the expected numbers.
  2. We confirm availability within two business days and invite you to see the hall.
  3. Sign the rental agreement and pay the $100 deposit to hold the date.
  4. Submit your floor plan, permit and insurance certificate at least 7 days before the event, and pay the balance 14 days before.
  5. Meet the custodian on the day for keys and a walk-through.

Hall rental inquiry

Inquiries go to the parish office. We reply within two business days. On WordPress this is a Form block.

Thank you. Your inquiry has been received and the office will be in touch within two business days.

Frequently asked

Can we bring our own caterer?

Yes. Any licensed caterer is welcome, and we can suggest several that know the kitchen. Caterers must be out and the kitchen clean by the end of your booking.

Can we come the day before to decorate?

If the hall is free, decorating time can be booked at the weekday daytime rate. Please ask when you book.

Is the hall available for non-Catholic groups?

Yes, for community events consistent with the parish's mission. Political fundraisers and events with content contrary to Church teaching are not accepted.

Questions? Contact Ann Marie O'Connor at 416-555-0142 ext. 20 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

item.title: Parish History
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Every parish is a story of people who decided that a church belonged where they lived. At St. Columba the story begins in the years after the Second World War, when East York's market gardens were giving way to streets of new brick houses and the families moving into them, many of them fresh off the boat from Cork, Calabria and Kerry, had a long walk to the nearest Catholic church. What follows is the short version. The long version lives in the memories of our older parishioners, and we are collecting it.

Timeline

  • 1954

    A parish is founded

    The Archbishop of Toronto established St. Columba Parish on September 12, 1954, carving it out of the territory of two older parishes. The first pastor, Fr. Michael Brennan, celebrated the first Mass on the following Sunday in the rented Orange Hall on Pape Avenue, an irony the Irish founders enjoyed for years. About 180 families registered in the first month.

  • 1956

    The parish hall

    Land on Columba Avenue was purchased and a plain cinder-block hall went up, built largely by volunteers on Saturdays. It served as church, school gym and social centre for five years, with Mass at the front and bingo at the back on Fridays.

  • 1961

    The church is dedicated

    The present church, designed in a modern Gothic style with a 32-metre bell tower, was dedicated on May 21, 1961. Parishioners paid for it with a building campaign that took seven years to retire; the Italian community donated the marble altar, and the Catholic Women's League furnished the sacristy.

  • 1970s

    Portuguese and Italian growth

    Immigration from the Azores and southern Italy changed the neighbourhood, and the parish with it. Sunday Mass in Italian began in 1972, and a Portuguese-speaking assistant priest arrived in 1976. The feast of Our Lady of Fátima procession, still held each May, dates from these years.

  • 1984

    Thirtieth anniversary

    The church was repainted, the pipe organ installed, and the parish choir formally founded under its first director. The St. Vincent de Paul conference opened its food cupboard in the hall basement.

  • 1990s

    Filipino and Spanish communities

    Newcomers from the Philippines, Colombia, El Salvador and Peru made the parish home. Mass in Tagalog began in 1993 and in Spanish in 1997. The Legion of Mary and the Simbang Gabi novena before Christmas both trace their beginnings here to this decade.

  • 2004

    Golden jubilee renovation

    For the fiftieth anniversary the sanctuary was reordered, the roof replaced and the stained glass restored. The Archbishop celebrated the jubilee Mass on September 12, 2004, exactly fifty years after the founding.

  • 2019

    Accessibility project

    A $1.4 million campaign funded the east-side accessible entrance, an elevator to the hall, accessible washrooms and a hearing loop, making every part of the parish available to every parishioner. Fr. Daniel Moreau arrived as pastor the same summer.

  • 2020–2021

    The pandemic

    With the church closed for long stretches, the parish learned to livestream Mass, deliver groceries to seniors and run Confirmation classes online. The livestream continues every Sunday at 11:00 AM.

  • 2024

    Seventieth anniversary

    Seventy years to the day after the first Mass, the parish gathered for a bilingual anniversary Mass, a photo exhibition in the hall and a dinner that sold out its 220 seats in a week. A Tamil community, the sixth language group, was formally welcomed the same year.

The church building

The church seats 540 and was built in a restrained modern Gothic style typical of Toronto parishes of the early 1960s: a tall brick nave, a narrow bell tower, and clear light from high windows. The three bells were cast in 1961 and are named for the founding pastor's parents and for St. Columba himself.

The stained glass, installed in stages between 1961 and 1974, tells the life of Christ down the north aisle and the lives of saints of the parish's founding nations down the south: Patrick, Brigid, Francis of Assisi, Anthony of Padua, Columba. A window of Our Lady of Fátima was added by the Portuguese community in 1980, and one of San Lorenzo Ruiz by the Filipino community in 2004.

Pastors of St. Columba

Help us keep the story

Parish archive project

We are gathering photographs, bulletins, wedding programs and memories from the parish's first decades. If you have a shoebox of pictures from a First Communion in 1965 or the hall's opening in 1956, we would love to scan them and give them back the same day. Contact the office at 416-555-0142 or office@stcolumbatoronto.ca. Selected images appear in the photo gallery.

The parish's sacramental registers, which go back to the first baptism in October 1954, are kept in the office. If you need a baptism, confirmation or marriage certificate, see Questions & Answers for how to request one.

item.title: New Here?
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Walking into an unfamiliar church can feel like arriving at a party where everyone else knows the steps. Please do not let that keep you away. Nobody at St. Columba will ask you to prove anything, and nobody minds if you sit at the back and watch. This page answers the questions visitors ask most often, so that you can arrive on Sunday knowing what to expect.

What happens at Mass

A Sunday Mass lasts about an hour (the 11:00 AM Mass with choir runs a little longer). The order is the same in every Catholic church in the world, so once you have been here once you will recognize it anywhere. Here is the shape of it.

  1. Arrive and find a seat

    Doors open thirty minutes before Mass. An usher near the entrance can hand you a hymn book and a bulletin. Any empty seat is yours; there are no reserved pews.

  2. Introductory rites

    We stand and sing as the priest and servers enter. There is a short prayer asking God's mercy and, on most Sundays, the Gloria.

  3. Liturgy of the Word

    We sit for two readings from the Bible and a psalm, then stand for the Gospel. The priest or deacon gives a homily of about ten minutes, and then we stand to say the Creed and pray for the world.

  4. Liturgy of the Eucharist

    Gifts of bread and wine are brought forward and the collection is taken. The priest prays the Eucharistic Prayer while we kneel. We stand to pray the Our Father and offer one another a sign of peace, usually a handshake or a nod.

  5. Holy Communion

    Catholics who have prepared come forward to receive. If you are not Catholic, or not ready, you are welcome to stay in your seat or to come forward with your arms crossed over your chest for a blessing.

  6. Sending forth

    A few announcements, a final blessing, and a closing hymn. Father Moreau or Father Nguyen greets people at the door afterwards. Please say hello.

What should I wear?

Whatever you would wear to visit a friend's home for a meal. You will see suits and you will see jeans. Bring nothing but yourself; there is no charge, and the collection is entirely voluntary.

Getting here

Parking

Our lot is behind the parish hall, with the entrance off Columba Avenue. It holds about sixty cars and fills up for the 11:00 AM Mass, so arrive early or plan on street parking. Columba Avenue and the side streets allow three-hour parking on Sundays; please respect the driveways of our neighbours. Four accessible spaces sit next to the east entrance.

TTC

Take Line 2 to Pape Station and walk north about eight minutes, or take the 25 Don Mills bus from the station to the stop at Columba Avenue, directly in front of the church. The 81 Thorncliffe Park bus also stops within two blocks.

Accessibility

The main doors on Columba Avenue have steps. The accessible entrance is on the east side of the church, with a push-button door and a ramp. Inside, the front pews on the left have cut-outs for wheelchairs and walkers. The church has a hearing loop; set your hearing aid to the T setting. An elevator connects the church level to the parish hall and the accessible washroom. Large-print hymn sheets are available from the ushers. Full details are on our accessibility page.

Families with children

Children belong at Mass, noise and all. If your little one needs a break, the cry room at the back left has a window, a speaker and a change table. During the 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM Masses from September to June, children aged four to nine are invited to Children's Liturgy of the Word: they leave after the opening prayer for a short reflection on the readings in the hall and return at the offertory. All leaders are screened under the Archdiocese's Safe Environment policy.

Washrooms, including a family washroom with a change table, are downstairs and beside the east entrance. See children and families for programs through the week.

Becoming a parishioner

You do not need to register to attend, but registering means we can issue tax receipts, send you envelopes, and know who you are when you ask for a baptism, wedding or letter of reference. It takes five minutes. Fill in the online registration form, pick up a paper form at the back of the church, or phone the office at 416-555-0142. We will send a welcome package within two weeks.

Register with the parish

Frequently asked questions

I am not Catholic. May I still come?

Yes. Everyone is welcome at Mass and at anything else we do. If you become curious about the faith itself, our Becoming Catholic page explains how adults explore it, with no commitment.

I have not been to church in years. Will anyone notice?

Only in the sense that we will be glad to see you. If you would like to talk to a priest about coming back, or to go to confession, see Reconciliation or phone the office for an appointment.

Which Mass should I choose?

Saturday 5:00 PM is quiet and quick. Sunday 9:00 AM draws many families with young children. The 11:00 AM has the full choir and is livestreamed. The 1:00 PM rotates between Spanish, Tagalog and Italian, and the 5:00 PM is led by young adults with contemporary music.

Is there coffee afterwards?

Yes, after the 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM Masses in the hall, hosted by the hospitality ministry. It is the easiest way to meet people.

Can I bring my service dog?

Of course. Service animals are welcome anywhere in the church and hall.

Still wondering about something? Email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca or ask an usher on Sunday. More answers are on our Questions & Answers page.

item.title: Our Faith
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
The Catholic faith is two thousand years old and practised by more than a billion people, but it is not complicated at its heart. God made the world and loves it. In Jesus Christ, God became one of us, died for us and rose from the dead. The Holy Spirit gathers us into the Church, feeds us with the sacraments and sends us out to love our neighbours. Everything else we teach and do grows from that. This section of the website is for anyone who wants to understand it better, whether you have been Catholic all your life or are looking in from outside for the first time.

What Catholics believe

Catholics believe in one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. We believe that Jesus of Nazareth is truly God and truly human, that he founded the Church on the apostles, and that he is really present in the Eucharist we celebrate at every Mass. We believe that the Bible is the inspired word of God, read and understood within the living tradition of the Church. We believe that every human being, from conception to natural death, carries the image of God and deserves dignity, and that we will be judged on how we treated the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner.

We also believe that faith is not a private possession. It is meant to be lived in a community, celebrated in the sacraments, and shared. That is why a parish exists.

Read more about beliefs and teachings

“Faith is not a set of answers to memorize. It is a person to meet, a table to sit at, and a road to walk together.”

Rev. Daniel Moreau, homily for the 70th anniversary

Five doors into the same room. Pick the one that fits your question.

For adults exploring the faith

OCIA is the unhurried path by which adults are baptized, received into the Church or confirmed. Tuesdays at 7:00 PM, September to Easter. No commitment to come and listen.

Growing in faith as an adult

Many Catholics stopped learning about their faith at Confirmation. The parish offers several ways to pick it up again. Sr. Agnes leads a Bible study on Wednesday mornings after the 8:30 Mass and a six-week adult formation series each Lent and Advent. The Alpha course, an informal ten-week exploration of the basics over dinner, runs every autumn. Formation for Discipleship, the Archdiocese's program for adults, offers online courses through the year. See faith formation for dates.

Have a question about the faith?

There is no such thing as a foolish question. Email Sr. Agnes Ibeh at faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca or ext. 25, or speak with either priest after Mass. If your question is about coming back to the Church after time away, Fr. Moreau would be glad to meet you privately.

item.title: Parish Councils
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Under Church law the pastor is responsible for the parish, but no pastor should carry that responsibility alone. Two councils and two committees, made up of parishioners who give their evenings for free, help Fr. Moreau read the needs of the community, spend its money wisely, keep the roof sound, and make sure people know what is going on. Their meetings are not secret. Minutes are posted on the bulletin board by the east entrance and summarized in the bulletin, and any parishioner can bring an item forward.

Parish Pastoral Council

The Pastoral Council is a consultative body that helps the pastor discern the direction of the parish. It does not run ministries or manage money; it listens, reflects and advises. Its main work over the past two years was the consultation that produced the 2025–2028 pastoral plan, and its main work now is helping the pastor keep that plan on track.

Members serve a three-year term, renewable once. Half are elected by parishioners at the annual parish meeting each May; half are appointed by the pastor so that every language community and age group has a voice.

Members by role

  • Chair — Grace Okafor, elected 2024
  • Vice-chair — Roberto Mendes, Portuguese community
  • Secretary — Jennifer Tan
  • Ex officio — Rev. Daniel Moreau (pastor), Rev. Joseph Nguyen, Deacon Paul Ferreira, Sr. Agnes Ibeh
  • Elected members — one representative each for liturgy, faith formation, outreach and social justice, youth and young adults
  • Appointed members — one representative each for the Spanish, Tagalog, Italian and Tamil communities, plus one for seniors

Meetings and raising an item

The council meets on the second Tuesday of the month, 7:30–9:00 PM, in the rectory meeting room, September through June. To raise an item, email the secretary at office@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "Pastoral Council" in the subject line at least one week before the meeting, or put a note in the suggestion box at the back of the church. You will get a written reply after the meeting, usually within two weeks.

Finance Council

Every parish in the Archdiocese of Toronto is required to have a Finance Council. Ours reviews the monthly accounts, prepares the annual budget, approves any spending over $5,000, oversees the annual review by the Archdiocese, and reports to parishioners each February. Members are appointed by the pastor for three-year terms and bring accounting, banking, legal and property experience. The current chair is Anthony Carvalho, CPA; the council meets on the third Wednesday of the month at 7:00 PM.

2025 financial summary

These figures are from the report presented at the February 2026 parish meeting. The full report, with notes, is available from the office.

Separately, parishioners gave $96,800 to ShareLife in 2025, exceeding our parish goal of $90,000. ShareLife funds are collected by the parish but passed entirely to the Archdiocese's charitable agencies and are not part of parish income. To support the parish, see ways to give.

Building & Maintenance Committee

A subcommittee of the Finance Council, this group of six parishioners with trades and engineering backgrounds walks the buildings twice a year, keeps a ten-year capital plan, gets quotes for major work and supervises contractors. Current priorities are the church roof (replacement scheduled for summer 2027), the hall kitchen, and converting the remaining lighting to LED. Chair: Frank Petrucci. Meets quarterly, or as projects require. Parishioners who notice a problem with the buildings should tell the office; the committee reviews every report.

Communications Committee

Formed in 2023, the Communications Committee looks after the weekly bulletin, this website, the parish email list, the livestream and the sign on Columba Avenue. It also helps ministries publicize their events and makes sure notices reach every language community. Members include a retired journalist, a graphic designer, two high-school students who run the livestream and the parish secretary. Chair: Priya Raman. Meets on the first Monday of the month at 7:00 PM. To submit a bulletin notice, email office@stcolumbatoronto.ca by Tuesday noon for the following weekend.

Serving on a council

Vacancies are announced in the bulletin each spring. Any registered parishioner over eighteen may stand for the Pastoral Council; the Finance Council seeks people with relevant professional experience. All members complete the Archdiocese's volunteer screening. If you would like to know more, speak with any council member after Mass or contact the office.

item.title: Parish School
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Toronto is one of the few places in the world where publicly funded Catholic schools sit at the heart of parish life. St. Columba Catholic School, part of the Toronto Catholic District School Board (TCDSB), opened in 1958 on Columba Avenue, just two blocks north of the church, and serves about 380 students from Junior Kindergarten to Grade 8. The parish and the school are separate institutions with one mission: to help children know Christ and grow into good, capable, generous people.

Sacramental preparation

In the Archdiocese of Toronto, the parish, not the school, prepares children for the sacraments, and families register through the parish. The school supports that preparation in religion class, where the Grade 2 curriculum covers Reconciliation and First Communion and the Grade 7 curriculum covers Confirmation. Sr. Agnes, our Catechetical Coordinator, meets the school's Grade 2 and Grade 7 teachers each September to align what is taught in class with what happens in the parish program. Children who attend other schools, including public schools, are equally welcome in our sacramental programs; see Sacramental Preparation.

How school and parish work together

  • School Masses. The whole school comes to the church for Mass at the opening of the year in September, on All Saints, in Advent, on Ash Wednesday, in Easter season and for the Grade 8 graduation Mass in June. Fr. Nguyen also celebrates a monthly Mass in the school gym for one division at a time. Parents are always welcome.
  • Chaplaincy. Fr. Nguyen serves as the school's parish priest liaison, visiting classrooms, leading Advent and Lent reconciliation services for Grades 3 to 8, and being available to families and staff. The school also has a TCDSB chaplaincy lead on staff who coordinates retreats and prayer life.
  • Catholic School Council. A parish representative, appointed by the pastor, sits on the school council; currently that is Deacon Ferreira.
  • Shared outreach. Students run a Lenten food drive for our St. Vincent de Paul conference, sing at the parish Christmas concert, and serve at the Sunday 9:00 AM Mass as altar servers and readers.
  • Youth ministry. Marcus Lee visits the Grade 7 and 8 classes each fall to invite students to the parish youth group, which is the bridge from elementary school to high school faith life.

Pastor's letter for school registration

Some TCDSB schools ask for proof of Catholic baptism at registration. If you need a baptismal certificate, or a letter from the pastor confirming that your family is registered with the parish, contact the office at 416-555-0142 ext. 20. Certificates take about a week; letters can usually be done in a day or two.

Registering at St. Columba Catholic School

Registration is handled by the school and the TCDSB, not the parish. Kindergarten registration for the following September opens each January, and families may register at any time during the year if they move into the area. To register a child you will generally need proof of the child's age (birth certificate or passport), proof of address, immunisation records, and, for Catholic admission, the child's or a parent's Catholic baptismal certificate. Contact the school office directly, or start online through the Board's website.

tcdsb.org

Catholic high schools

Graduates of St. Columba Catholic School go on to TCDSB secondary schools across the east end of the city, including the Catholic high schools closest to East York and the Board's specialty programs in the arts, technology and French immersion. Open houses take place in October and November, and Grade 8 families receive information from the school in the fall. Our parish youth group and 5:00 PM Sunday Mass are where many of our teens stay connected to the parish after they scatter to different high schools; see Youth Ministry.

Rosary Apostolate in the schools

Once a month from October to May, volunteers from the Rosary Apostolate visit every classroom at St. Columba Catholic School to pray a decade of the rosary with the children and teach them about the mysteries and the life of Mary. The Apostolate is a lay movement active across the Archdiocese; our parish team has nine members and is led by Concetta Bruno (rosary@stcolumbatoronto.ca). Volunteers complete high-risk screening and a short training session in September. It is a wonderful ministry for retirees and for parents with a free weekday morning.

Frequently asked

My child attends a public school. Can they still make First Communion here?

Yes. Sacramental preparation happens through the parish, and about a quarter of the children in our programs attend public or private schools. Register in September through the parish office.

Do we have to be parishioners to attend the school?

No. Admission is set by the TCDSB. But families who worship here find the connection between school and parish much richer, and registering with the parish is simple; see Register with the Parish.

Does the school have before- and after-school care?

Ask the school office; child-care programs in TCDSB schools are run by licensed providers and change from year to year.

Can our family attend the school Masses?

Always. They are announced in the bulletin and on the school's newsletter, and there is room at the back of the church.

Questions about the parish's work with the school? Contact Sr. Agnes Ibeh at 416-555-0142 ext. 25 or faith@stcolumbatoronto.ca.

item.title: Pastoral Plan
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
In the autumn of 2024, as the parish marked its seventieth anniversary, the Pastoral Council asked a simple question: what should St. Columba look like at seventy-five? More than four hundred parishioners answered, through listening sessions in six languages, a survey, and conversations after every Mass for two months. This plan is what we heard, distilled into five priorities. It was approved by Fr. Moreau and the Pastoral Council in January 2025 and covers three years. Each priority has three goals and a measure so that the parish can see, honestly, whether it is getting there.

Our vision

“By 2028, St. Columba will be a parish where every person who walks through the door is known by name, formed in the faith, and sent out to serve East York in the love of Christ.”

Vision statement, Pastoral Plan 2025–2028

Five priorities

What we will do

The order below is not a ranking. Worship comes first because everything else flows from the altar.

1. Worship: celebrate the liturgy with reverence and joy

  • Train and commission 40 new liturgical ministers (lectors, extraordinary ministers of Communion, ushers, servers) by June 2026, so that no ministry depends on the same twelve people.
  • Establish a second choir for the 9:00 AM Mass by Advent 2026, and grow the youth choir to 25 singers.
  • Add a monthly Mass in Tamil by 2027 and provide printed worship aids in all six languages for Christmas and Easter.

Measure: the number of active liturgical ministers in the parish database, reported to the Pastoral Council each June, and the October count of Mass attendance required by the Archdiocese.

2. Formation: help every age grow in faith

  • Offer at least one adult formation series every Advent and Lent and run the Alpha course every autumn, with a goal of 120 adults participating each year.
  • Re-launch the parish's sacramental preparation for First Communion and Confirmation with a family-based model by September 2026, so that parents are formed alongside their children.
  • Ensure every catechist and youth leader completes the Archdiocese's Formation for Discipleship foundations course by 2027.

Measure: annual participation counts for adult programs; percentage of catechists with completed formation, reported by Sr. Agnes each September.

3. Community: know one another by name

  • Build a team of welcomers so that a greeter is at every door at every weekend Mass, and every newly registered family receives a personal visit or call within a month.
  • Hold one parish-wide social event each season that brings the language communities together, beginning with a multicultural food festival in June 2025.
  • Launch a seniors' outreach so that every homebound parishioner is visited at least monthly and receives Communion if they wish.

Measure: new registrations per year and the share contacted within 30 days; the number of homebound parishioners on the visiting list and visits logged.

4. Outreach: serve East York

  • Expand the St. Vincent de Paul food cupboard to open twice a week and increase households served from 40 to 60 a month by 2027.
  • Sponsor one refugee family through the Office for Refugees of the Archdiocese of Toronto in each year of the plan.
  • Partner with the two parish schools and a local seniors' residence on a yearly service project involving the youth group.

Measure: households served and food distributed, from the St. Vincent de Paul conference's annual report; refugee families welcomed; youth service hours logged.

5. Stewardship: care for what we have been given

  • Increase the share of households giving through Pre-Authorized Giving from 22 per cent to 40 per cent by 2028, so that parish income is stable through the summer and winter.
  • Complete the church roof replacement in 2027 from the capital reserve without a special campaign, and convert all lighting to LED.
  • Publish a plain-language financial report every February and post Pastoral and Finance Council minutes within two weeks of each meeting.

Measure: PAG participation rate and capital reserve balance, from the Finance Council's annual report; minutes posted on time.

How you can help

Give an hour a month

Most of the goals above need people more than money. Welcomers, lectors, drivers for seniors, food cupboard volunteers and catechists are the plan's engine.

Volunteer

Sign up for PAG

Pre-Authorized Giving takes five minutes to set up and means the parish can plan. You choose the amount; you can change it any time.

Ways to give

Come to a formation series

The plan will only work if parishioners keep learning. Join Alpha this autumn or the Lenten series, and bring a neighbour.

Faith formation

Keeping ourselves honest

The Pastoral Council reviews progress on every goal each June and reports to the parish at the annual parish meeting in the hall, where any parishioner may ask questions. A one-page scorecard appears in the bulletin every September. Goals that are not working will be changed rather than quietly forgotten; the plan is a tool, not a monument. Questions or suggestions may go to any council member or to office@stcolumbatoronto.ca with "Pastoral Plan" in the subject line. See parish councils for how the council works.

Read the full plan

The complete document runs to twelve pages, with the consultation findings, the theology behind each priority, and the full list of measures. Printed copies are available at the back of the church.

On this demonstration site the download is a sample PDF, not the pastoral plan itself.

item.title: Prayers
item.dc:creator: parishoffice
item.content:encoded:
Prayer is simply talking with God and letting God talk with you. It can be done in your own words at the kitchen sink, and it can be done with words the Church has prayed for centuries. The set prayers below are the ones you will hear at Mass, at a bedside, at a graveside and in the pews before the 8:30 Mass when the Rosary is said. Learn them and you will never be at a loss for words when you need them. Click any prayer to open its text.

Common prayers

The Sign of the Cross

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Made with the right hand, touching the forehead, the chest, the left shoulder and the right shoulder. It begins and ends almost every Catholic prayer.

The Our Father (the Lord's Prayer)

Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.

The Hail Mary

Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen.

The Glory Be

Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

The Apostles' Creed

I believe in God, the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Amen.

Act of Contrition

O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended thee, and I detest all my sins because of thy just punishments, but most of all because they offend thee, my God, who art all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of thy grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasions of sin. Amen.

Said in the confessional after confessing your sins. Any sincere expression of sorrow in your own words is also acceptable. See Reconciliation.

Hail, Holy Queen (Salve Regina)

Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve; to thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. Turn, then, most gracious advocate, thine eyes of mercy toward us, and after this our exile show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. Pray for us, O holy Mother of God, that we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ. Amen.

Prayer to St. Michael the Archangel

St. Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle. Be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil. May God rebuke him, we humbly pray; and do thou, O Prince of the heavenly host, by the power of God, cast into hell Satan and all the evil spirits who prowl about the world seeking the ruin of souls. Amen.

Grace before meals

Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

After meals: We give thee thanks, almighty God, for all thy benefits, who livest and reignest for ever and ever. Amen.

Parish prayer to St. Columba

St. Columba, who left the shore of your own country to carry the light of Christ to a people not your own, pray for this parish of travellers and their children. Teach us to make a home for the stranger, to keep the faith in a new land, and to sail wherever the Lord sends us without fear. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

Written for the parish's 70th anniversary and prayed at the end of the Prayer of the Faithful on our patronal feast, June 9.

How to pray the Rosary

The Rosary is a meditation on twenty scenes, called mysteries, from the lives of Jesus and Mary, prayed on a string of beads. It takes about twenty minutes and is prayed in the church every weekday after the 8:30 AM Mass; anyone may join, and there are spare rosaries in the basket by the Mary altar. Beginners often find it easiest to pray with the group a few times before trying alone.

  1. Begin

    Holding the crucifix, make the Sign of the Cross and pray the Apostles' Creed. On the first bead pray an Our Father; on the next three, a Hail Mary each (for faith, hope and love); then a Glory Be.

  2. Announce the first mystery

    Say the name of the mystery (for example, "the first Joyful Mystery, the Annunciation") and picture the scene for a moment. Pray an Our Father on the large bead.

  3. Pray the decade

    Pray a Hail Mary on each of the ten small beads while keeping the mystery in mind, then a Glory Be. Many add the Fátima prayer: "O my Jesus, forgive us our sins, save us from the fires of hell, and lead all souls to heaven, especially those most in need of thy mercy."

  4. Repeat for five mysteries

    Announce the next mystery, Our Father, ten Hail Marys, Glory Be, and so on around the beads.

  5. Finish

    Pray the Hail, Holy Queen, then the Sign of the Cross. Some add a prayer for the Pope's intentions or for a particular need.

The mysteries by day of the week

During Advent and Christmas the Joyful Mysteries are often prayed on Sundays, and during Lent the Sorrowful.

The Divine Mercy Chaplet

The Chaplet is prayed on ordinary rosary beads and takes about seven minutes. It was given to St. Faustina Kowalska in the 1930s and is prayed in our parish at 3:00 PM on Fridays in Lent and on Divine Mercy Sunday, the Sunday after Easter. Its shape:

  • Begin with the Sign of the Cross, an Our Father, a Hail Mary and the Apostles' Creed.
  • On each large bead: "Eternal Father, I offer you the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of your dearly beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in atonement for our sins and those of the whole world."
  • On each of the ten small beads: "For the sake of his sorrowful Passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world."
  • After five decades, three times: "Holy God, Holy Mighty One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us and on the whole world."

Prayer in the parish

Rosary weekdays after the 8:30 AM Mass · Novena to Our Lady of Perpetual Help Wednesdays at 7:30 PM · Adoration Thursdays 9:00 AM–12:00 PM and First Fridays 7:00–8:00 PM. The church is open for private prayer from 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM on weekdays. To ask the parish to pray for someone, use the prayer request form; to have a Mass offered, see Mass intentions. More on devotions and Adoration.
